units.title: Basics: jobs and Burst
units.blurb: Two separate things — threads and a compiler, what Burst can and cannot compile, the kinds of jobs and Schedule versus Run versus Complete. This is where they check you have really used them.

lessons.title: Schedule, Run, Complete
lessons.sub: When a job really runs, and why Complete() right after Schedule() is a mistake

cards.title: Schedule queues the job and returns a JobHandle
cards.body:
Schedule() does not run the job. It copies the job struct, puts it in a queue and immediately returns a JobHandle — a receipt you later use to wait for the result or to make another job depend on this one.

A detail not everyone knows: by default the job goes into a local queue and the worker threads do not see it yet. Unity batches jobs on purpose, because waking threads is expensive. The work reaches the workers when you call JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs() or Complete().

So between Schedule() and Complete() the main thread is free — that gap is the whole point of jobs.

cards.title: Run, Schedule, Complete — three verbs
cards.body:
Run() executes Execute right away, on the same thread, with no queue and no parallelism. Under Burst it is still fast, and it is handy for debugging and for small data.

Schedule() — put it in the queue and get a JobHandle.

Complete() — wait. It raises the priority of the job and all its dependencies, and if no worker has picked the job up yet, it runs it right on the calling thread. Complete() also clears the safety system marks on the containers: until the job is completed with Complete(), the main thread may not read or write its data.

handle.IsCompleted only tells you whether the job has finished; it does not replace Complete().
cards.code:
job.Run();                        // here and now, on this thread
JobHandle h = job.Schedule(n, 64); // queued
// ... the main thread does its own work ...
h.Complete();                     // wait; the data is safe to read

cards.q: What do you get if you call Complete() on the very next line after Schedule()?
options: The speed of Run() plus the scheduling overhead: no parallelism with the main thread
Double speed: the main thread helps the workers
cards.explain: Between Schedule() and Complete() the main thread does nothing, so it just waits. An IJobParallelFor still spreads its iterations over the workers, but the main thread idles the whole time, and you paid for queueing. There is no safety error here — it is not a race, it is lost parallelism.

wrong.1: Complete() can indeed run the job on the main thread, but that gains nothing: the main thread did none of its own work.
wrong.2: You get an exception when you touch the job data before Complete(). Here the order is right, just pointless.
wrong.3: Complete() blocks until the job is done, right now.

cards.title: Schedule early, complete late
cards.body:
The rule: schedule early, complete late. Schedule the job as soon as its input is ready, and call Complete() as late as you can — when you actually need the result.

The classic example from Unity’s docs: Schedule() in Update, Complete() in LateUpdate. In between run every other script’s Update, animation and physics — and all that time the worker threads compute your job.

Keep the JobHandle in a field for that. Right after Schedule() call JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs(), or the job may sit in the local queue until Complete().

cards.q: Which line kills parallelism in this frame?
cards.explain: Complete() comes right after Schedule(), so UpdateAI and UpdateUI wait for the job to end. Move Complete() to where the result is needed — LateUpdate, or at least after UpdateAI and UpdateUI — and the main thread works in parallel with the workers.

cards.q: What is true about Complete()? Pick all that apply.
options: If the job has not started, it may run right on the thread that called Complete()
Complete() also completes every job this one depends on
If you check handle.IsCompleted, you do not have to call Complete()
Until Complete() is called, the main thread must not read or write the job’s data
cards.explain: Complete() raises the priority of the job and its dependencies and may run it on the calling thread. Until it is called, the safety system treats the data as busy, and reading it on the main thread throws in the editor. IsCompleted only reports readiness: Complete() is still needed, it clears the safety system marks. Complete() returns no result — the result sits in the container you passed into the job.

cards.task: Rewrite Scaler so the job runs in parallel with the rest of the frame: Schedule in Update, Complete and Use(output) in LateUpdate. Keep the JobHandle in a field and wake the worker threads right after Schedule.

checks.label: The JobHandle is a field of the class, not a local of Update
JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs() is called right after Schedule
There is a LateUpdate method that calls Complete()
Use(output) is called in LateUpdate after Complete()

cards.explain: The job starts in Update while the rest of the frame’s scripts run, and by LateUpdate it is usually done — Complete() just collects the result.

cards.title: So why Run()
cards.body:
Run() is not a “bad Schedule”. It is the same job and the same Burst code, executed here and now on the current thread.

It fits when the data is small and queueing costs more than the work, when you need the result immediately, and when debugging: the order of execution becomes predictable while the Burst code stays Burst code.

If you are going to write Schedule() and then Complete() right away anyway, write Run() instead: same meaning, no scheduling.
cards.code:
// small data, result needed right now
new ScaleJob { input = input, output = output, k = 2f }.Run(input.Length);

cards.q: Put one “schedule early, complete late” frame in order.
items: Update: gather the input into a NativeArray
Other Updates, animation, physics — the workers compute the job
LateUpdate: read the result and apply it
cards.explain: The data is ready — schedule the job at once and wake the threads. Everything between Update and LateUpdate runs in parallel. Complete() comes last, right before reading the result.

cards.task: Fix Update: the result is read before the job has finished, and the array is freed while the job may still write to it. Add the missing call in the right place.

checks.label: Complete() is called on the JobHandle
The array is still freed with Dispose()

cards.explain: In the editor the safety system would catch reading result[0] before Complete() with an exception. A build has no such checks: you would read garbage, and Dispose() would free memory the job is still writing. Here you have to wait at once because the result is needed in this same Update; when you can, move the read to LateUpdate.

cards.q: Interviewer: “Your job takes 2 ms, you Schedule in Update and Complete in LateUpdate, yet the profiler shows LateUpdate waiting 2 ms.” What do you check first?
options: Whether JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs() is called after Schedule: without it the job may have sat in the local queue until Complete()
Whether Burst is on — Complete() does not work without it
Whether there are too many worker threads
cards.explain: If the worker threads were never woken, the job starts only in Complete(), and all 2 ms land on LateUpdate. Check ScheduleBatchedJobs first, then look at the profiler Timeline to see when the job actually started on the workers.
